results.title: Decision Curve Analysis for Model Evaluation • dcurves
results.content: # Decision Curve Analysis. Diagnostic and prognostic models are typically evaluated with measures of accuracy that do not address clinical consequences. Decision-analytic techniques allow assessment of clinical outcomes but often require collection of additional information and may be cumbersome to apply to models that yield a continuous result. Decision curve analysis is a method for evaluating and comparing prediction models that incorporates clinical consequences, requires only the data set on which the models are tested, and can be applied to models that have either continuous or dichotomous results. The **dcurves** package includes methods for evaluating predictive models with binary (Vickers and Elkin 2006) and time-to-event endpoints (Vickers et al. The package also includes methods for model evaluation in the case-control setting (Pfeiffer and Gail 2020). ## Installation. results.title: Decision curve for decision tree model
results.content: # Decision curve for decision tree model. Since there is only one true positive and one false positive (as oppose to with a continuous model outcome / predicted probability where these would vary depending on cut-points) the only thing that changes when calculating the net benefit across the thresholds of the decision curve, is the weighting applied to the false positives. I’m also unsure of how the model outcome would relate to the decision curve thresholds. output.tree <- ctree(nativeSpeaker ~ age + shoeSize + score, data = input.dat). input.dat$pred <- predict(output.tree). dca_object <- dca(nativeSpeaker ~ pred, data = input.dat). From your decision tree, you can either give a probability of 1 for “positive” individuals and 0 for “negatives” or give a probability based on observed probabilities (e.g. if there are 50 individuals at a given terminal node on your tree, and 16 of them have the event, that is a probability of 32%). In the code included in my original post, I used 0 or 1 as the probability to feed into the decision curve to give the curve ‘Pred’:. input.dat$node <- attributes(output.tree)$where. dca_object_prob <- dca(nativeSpeaker ~ prob, data = input.dat). The curve for the model (above shown as Prob) plateaus at 69% (i.e. the only non-0/1 probability) since there are no false positives after this point. If instead of giving probability of 1 and 0 to positive and negative tests, you give probabilities of the PPV and 1-PPV, then the decision curve follows the “treat all” line until threshold probability is 1-NPV, then has higher net benefit until it hits the x axis at threshold probability of PPV, and then follows the x axis. Re the blue line, the example tree has 4 terminal nodes, I’d used the probability for each node rather than overall, which is what you get from the model if you use the ‘predict’ command…. If I use the overall PPV i.e. cm <- confusionMatrix(input.dat$pred, input.dat$nativeSpeaker, positive = "yes"). I think this is the same as my original attempt, having thought about it though, should the probability be assigned relative to what the node is predicting for example node 4 is predicting an outcome of ‘no’ so should the probability be 1 i.e. the model correctly classified 13/13?

results.title: Decision Curve Analysis Explained | medRxiv
results.content: By plotting the net benefit of each strategy across a range of threshold probabilities, the decision curve shows whether and when a model provides higher clinical utility than blanket treatment or no treatment at all. The model provides clinical benefit only in the range of thresholds where its curve lies above both reference strategies. To illustrate the application of decision curve analysis (DCA) in pediatric diagnostic research, a synthetic dataset was constructed simulating a cohort of pediatric patients evaluated in the Emergency Department for abdominal pain with suspected acute appendicitis (Supplementary File 1). The PAS score demonstrated a consistent and clinically meaningful net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities, clearly outperforming both the “treat-all” and “treat-none” strategies, except at very high thresholds (>0.9), where the curve converged with “treat none” as expected given the simulated prevalence. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC, upper panels) and decision curve analysis (DCA, lower panels) for three predictors of acute appendicitis in a simulated pediatric emergency cohort (n=200, prevalence 20%). Its DCA curve largely overlapped with the “treat-none” and “treat-all” strategies across thresholds, with only a minimal interval of apparent net benefit around 0.2–0.3, underscoring its lack of practical utility despite AUC values commonly reported in the literature. In DCA, PAS consistently provided greater net benefit than either “treat-all” or “treat-none” across almost the entire range of thresholds, except beyond 0.9, where convergence with “treat none” occurred as expected given the simulated prevalence. At a simulated prevalence of 5%, the decision curve showed broad overlap with the “treat none” strategy beyond a threshold probability of 0.5, reflecting the scarcity of true positive cases and the growing penalty of false positives as thresholds increase. Conversely, at a simulated prevalence of 70%, the curve demonstrated consistently high net benefit, exceeding both “treat all” and “treat none” strategies across the entire threshold range. At a prevalence of 70%, the curve shows consistently high net benefit, remaining above both “treat all” and “treat none” across the full range of thresholds, as expected when baseline risk is high and true positives predominate. It highlights DCA’s focus on clinical utility—quantifying net benefit across decision thresholds—and its ability to compare models against “treat-all” and “treat-none” strategies.

results.title: Pros :) and Cons :( of Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) for Clinical Decision-Making
results.content:
Pros :) and Cons :( of Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) for Clinical Decision-Making
Saniya Khullar
1470 subscribers
24 likes
1635 views
31 Dec 2021
Decision Curve Analysis (DCA), is a novel approach (that improves upon traditional predictive machine learning model evaluation approaches like Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, etc. for evaluating the clinical net benefit of using various prediction models) that was developed by Dr. Andrew J. Vickers and Dr. Elena B. Elkins (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17099194/) in November, 2006. That is, DCA is a powerful approach for evaluating the costs of a False Positive (FP:  wrongly predicting a patient has a disease when they actually do not (and are healthy)...patient incurs unnecessary treatment and side effects, cost, stress, etc.) and a False Negative (FN: wrongly predicting that a diseased patient is instead healthy...patient's condition could deteriorate; for example the cancer could progress to advanced stage).  DCA allows us to evaluate models based on how we weigh the costs of FP and FN mistakes, subjectively, using the notion of probability thresholds. For more clarity on probability thresholds, please see Saniya's video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VJOq_ezsOIs&t=15s.

In this video, Saniya focuses on the main Pros (strengths :) ) as well as the main Cons (weaknesses :( ) of Decision Curve Analysis.  Please note that these are important things to be considered.  And often, DCA works well in conjunction with other model evaluation approaches.  So, Saniya humbly believes that while DCA is indeed an invaluable tool, other machine learning evaluation models do hold their own merits and should also be used for a more holistic evaluation. 

Also, please note that this was not mentioned in the video, but Saniya wanted to add that although i mention there is no main method for correcting decision curve analysis for being overfit, there are some different methods for correcting for overfit models (https://bmcmedinformdecismak.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1472-6947-8-53): 
"We therefore recommend repeated 10-fold cross-validation as a method to correct decision curves created using the same data as that used to generate the model.'

Further, to clarify: A net benefit of x means that your model / test / whatever is the equivalent of a strategy that found 100 x for every 100 patients without any patient having a false positive. For instance, if the decision curve is about cancer biopsy, and at a given threshold net benefit for a model was 0.20, you'd say that using the model is the equivalent of doing 20 biopsies per 100 and every single one had cancer, there were no negative biopsies. You can say the same about difference in net benefit. In the biopsy example, if the net benefit between model A and model B was 0.01 at a 10% threshold, you'd say that using model A rather than model B was the equivalent of finding one extra cancer per 100 for the same number of biopsies. You can also convert difference in net benefit to the unit of false positives, rather than true positives but dividing net benefit by pt /(1 – pt). so our difference between model A and model B would be 0.09 and you could say "using model A rather than model B is the equivalent of doing 9 fewer biopsies per 100 but finding the same number of cancers".

Saniya does have other introductory videos on DCA and examples of the application of DCA so please do see Saniya's playlist on Decision Curve Analysis (DCA): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL_3UUp3wcnVYYQUQ5wXgNjkl1LI1mocA3

In this video, Saniya is mostly focused on how to interpret the net benefit on the treated in clinical terms and goes over the example provided in the paper by Vickers et. al.  

Please subscribe to Saniya's YouTube channel for more updates :).  Please reach out with any and all questions and concerns ye may have.  Also, to learn more about Decision Curve Analysis, please do check out this link: www.decisioncurveanalysis.org
